tools.name: check_offer_policy
tools.description:
Check an edited negotiation policy: returns {ok, policy, issues, summary}. No model call, free.

USE THIS WHEN: you changed a policy from compile_offer_policy (a floor, an option, a forbidden combination)
and want to know it is valid and what it now allows before using it in draft_negotiation_reply.

tools.name: verify_deal_receipt
tools.description:
Verify a signed deal receipt against the seller's own policy: both signatures, that the signing keys are
SNHP's own (published at /.well-known/ucp), the policy digest, and every rule re-checked from the package.
Returns {ok, problems, checks, signed_by_snhp, signatures}. Free, no model call.

findings.title: Description issues instructions to the model
findings.detail: Description of "check_offer_policy" contains imperative instructions directed at the AI assistant rather than describing the tool. This is the core tool-poisoning technique.

findings.remediation: Treat the server as untrusted; the model may obey embedded instructions.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta: untrusted input + private data + external sink
findings.detail: Server "mcp" exposes tools that together enable an exfiltration flow. Untrusted content: compile_offer_policy, draft_negotiation_reply, check_offer_policy · Private data: draft_negotiation_reply · Public sink: draft_negotiation_reply.

evidence.snippet: Untrusted content: compile_offer_policy, draft_negotiation_reply, check_offer_policy · Private data: draft_negotiation_reply · Public sink: draft_negotiation_reply

findings.remediation: Do not co-install these capabilities under one trust boundary; an injected comment/email can steer the model to exfiltrate via the sink tool.

findings.title: Tool description changed since last scan
findings.detail: Tool "draft_negotiation_reply" changed its description with no version change. Silent description changes are how a trusted server turns malicious after review.
